power.title: Power Analysis Check
report:
::: {.callout-tip title="Learn More" collapse="true"}

Power analyses need to contain the following information to be interpretable: the type of power analysis, the statistical test, the software used, sample size, critical alpha criterion, power level, effect size, and an effect size metric. In addition, it is recommended to make sure the power analysis is reproducible (by sharing the code, or a screenshot, of the power analysis), and to provide good arguments for why the study was designed to detect an effect of this size.

For an a-priori power analysis, where the sample size is determined, reporting all information would look like:

> An a priori power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that for a Cohen's d = 0.5, an alpha level of 0.05, and a desired power level of 80% required at least 64 participants in each group.

For a sensitivity power analysis, this sentence would look like:

> A sensitivity power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that with 64 participants in each group, and an alpha level of 0.05, a desired power level of 80% was reached for an effect size of d = 0.5.

:::

stat_p_nonsig.report: Meta-scientific research has shown nonsignificant p values are commonly misinterpreted. It is incorrect to infer that there is 'no effect', 'no difference', or that groups are 'the same' after p > 0.05. It is possible that there is a true non-zero effect, but that the study did not detect it. Make sure your inference acknowledges that it is possible that there is a non-zero effect. It is correct to include the effect is 'not significantly' different, although this just restates that p > 0.05. Metacheck does not yet analyze automatically whether sentences which include non-significant p-values are correct, but we recommend manually checking the sentences below for possible misinterpreted non-significant p values. ```{r} #| echo: false # table data -------------------------------------- table <- structure(list(Text = "p = 0.43", Sentence = "64.7%; p = 0.43; Fig 1C)."), row.names = c(NA, -1L), class = c("tbl_df", "tbl", "data.frame")) # display table ----------------------------------- metacheck::report_table(table, c(0.1, 0.9), 10, FALSE) ``` ::: {.callout-tip title="Learn More" collapse="true"} For metascientific articles demonstrating the rate of misinterpretations of non-significant results is high, see: Aczel B, Palfi B, Szollosi A, Kovacs M, Szaszi B, Szecsi P, Zrubka M, Gronau Q, van den Bergh D, Wagenmakers E (2018). “Quantifying Support for the Null Hypothesis in Psychology: An Empirical Investigation.” Advances in Methods and Practices in Psychological Science, 1(3), 357–366. doi:10.1177/2515245918773742. info.title: Can AI Scale Human Fact-Checking? Evidence from Community Notes

author.affiliation:
Oxford Internet Institute
								University of Oxford

Massachusetts Institute of Technology
								Sloan School of Management

text.text: Community Notes-a crowd-based fact-checking program through which social media users can flag a post with a note explaining why the post is misleading, and the note is displayed if a diverse set of users rate the note as helpful-has become central to online content moderation.
The program, however, faces substantial scalability constraints, as the generation of notes takes considerable time and effort, and the number of user participants is limited.
Here, we investigate whether allowing AI models to write Community Notes helps to alleviate these constraints by analyzing the full corpus of AI-generated Community Notes on X through May 2026.

Encouragingly, AI-generated notes are submitted more quickly, are longer, and cite more and higher-quality sources than human-written notes, while being rated helpful at a similar rate and being associated with similar decreases in reposts following the publication of a rated-helpful note.

Furthermore, a pre-registered survey experiment finds no statistically detectable difference between AI-and human-generated fact-checks in their effect on belief updating, regardless of whether the author was revealed to participants.

On the other hand, AI-generated note writing is highly concentrated, as a handful of accounts produce the large majority of notes, and are significantly less likely to engage with posts involving controversial and polarized topics such as politics and elections.

While those findings suggest that AI may be a powerful tool for scaling crowd-based fact-checking systems such as Community Notes, this evolution also entails important risks: shifting the primary bottleneck from note production to note evaluation, moving the system from a decentralized toward a more centralized model, and creating incentives to prioritize claims that are more likely to achieve consensus over those of greater societal importance.
Identifying false and misleading claims at scale is challenging because of the massive volume of content posted online every day.

While professional fact-checking is highly effective when applied (1), this approach does not scale: there are relatively few professional fact-checkers, and professional fact-checking is time-consuming and expensive.
text.formatted: While professional fact-checking is highly effective when applied <ref type="bibr" target="#b0">(1)</ref>, this approach does not scale: there are relatively few professional fact-checkers, and professional fact-checking is time-consuming and expensive.

text.text: Harnessing the "wisdom of crowds" has been proposed as a way to increase the scope and speed of fact-checking (2-4).

A prominent example of this approach is Community Notes, first deployed on X (formerly Twitter), with similar systems subsequently introduced by Meta (on Facebook, Instagram and Threads), TikTok and YouTube.
These systems allow volunteer contributors to evaluate potentially misleading posts and attach a brief, sourced correction that is displayed to all users once a consensus emerges (5).
text.formatted: These systems allow volunteer contributors to evaluate potentially misleading posts and attach a brief, sourced correction that is displayed to all users once a consensus emerges <ref type="bibr" target="#b4">(5)</ref>.

text.text: A growing body of experimental and observational evidence indicates that crowd-sourced factchecking can effectively identify (for a review, see (4)) and reduce the spread of (6, 7) false and misleading content on social media platforms.
text.formatted: A growing body of experimental and observational evidence indicates that crowd-sourced factchecking can effectively identify (for a review, see <ref type="bibr" target="#b3">(4)</ref>) and reduce the spread of (6, 7) false and misleading content on social media platforms.

text.text: Yet crowd-sourced fact-checking turns out to face a similar structural capacity constraint as professional fact-checking: even though there are more Community Notes contributors than professional fact-checkers, the volume of potentially misleading content still far exceeds what a volunteer community can feasibly review.

Only a small fraction of posts ever receive a published note, and notes that do appear arrive, on average, many hours after a post begins to circulate-long after much of the viral diffusion has already occurred and many users have already been exposed to it (6).
text.formatted: Only a small fraction of posts ever receive a published note, and notes that do appear arrive, on average, many hours after a post begins to circulate-long after much of the viral diffusion has already occurred and many users have already been exposed to it <ref type="bibr" target="#b5">(6)</ref>.

text.text: This latency problem is particularly consequential because misinformation diffuses fastest in its earliest hours (8).
text.formatted: This latency problem is particularly consequential because misinformation diffuses fastest in its earliest hours <ref type="bibr" target="#b7">(8)</ref>.

text.text: The emergence of large language models (LLMs), which can evaluate claims and generate text almost instantly, opens a potential path to addressing this bottleneck.

Although earlier LLMs had limited success at fact-checking (9), evidence suggests that current models can identify false and misleading claims as well as, or better than, a professional fact-checker (10).
text.formatted: Although earlier LLMs had limited success at fact-checking <ref type="bibr" target="#b8">(9)</ref>, evidence suggests that current models can identify false and misleading claims as well as, or better than, a professional fact-checker <ref type="bibr" target="#b9">(10)</ref>.

text.text: Thus, LLMs may be able to help satisfy the need for large-scale, in-the-moment provisioning of Community Notes.
Accordingly, X recently introduced a feature allowing "AI Note Writers" to submit AI-generated Community Notes (11, 12).
text.formatted: Accordingly, X recently introduced a feature allowing "AI Note Writers" to submit AI-generated Community Notes <ref type="bibr" target="#b10">(11,</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b11">12)</ref>.

text.text: Importantly, some AI Note Writers are operated internally by X while others are developed independently by external individuals or organizations (we ourselves have developed two AI Note Writers).

Once submitted, AI-generated notes follow the same process as human-written notes: they are evaluated by human contributors and become publicly visible only if rated as helpful by contributors who have historically disagreed in their evaluations of other notes.
When Community Notes participants rate proposed notes, whether a note is AI-generated is disclosed alongside the note text in the rating interface.

Once a note reaches "Currently Rated Helpful" status and is displayed on X, however, AI-generated and human-generated notes are displayed identically beneath the post: both carry the standard "Community Notes" label with no visible authorship information in the default view.

AI authorship is only disclosed in the note detail panel, which readers must actively open; there, AI-authored notes include the disclaimer: "Proposed by an experimental AI contributor responding to requests for a note.
Like all contributors, AIs can make mistakes-verify accuracy."
Human-authored notes carry no equivalent disclaimer (see Extended Data Fig. S1).
text.formatted: Human-authored notes carry no equivalent disclaimer (see Extended Data Fig. <ref type="figure" target="#fig_2">S1</ref>).

text.text: Here, we evaluate the promise and perils of the introduction of AI Note Writers by analyzing all Community Notes proposed on X between September 2025 (when AI note generation was introduced) and May 2026, complemented by an audit of our own admitted AI Note Writer to observe the note-production process from the inside and a preregistered survey experiment to causally identify whether revealing AI authorship changes belief updating.
Until recently, Community Notes could only be submitted by human volunteers enrolled in the program.
Beginning in September 2025,foot_0 X expanded Community Notes by allowing developers and users to create AI-powered note writers capable of drafting proposed notes on platform content.
text.formatted: Beginning in September 2025,<ref type="foot" target="#foot_0">foot_0</ref> X expanded Community Notes by allowing developers and users to create AI-powered note writers capable of drafting proposed notes on platform content.

text.text: Our dataset comprises 311,225 English-language notes indicating that an initial claim is misleading (68,978 AI-written and 242,247 human-written) proposed on 244,213 distinct posts between September 1, 2025, and May 12, 2026 (see Extended Data Fig. S2).
text.formatted: Our dataset comprises 311,225 English-language notes indicating that an initial claim is misleading (68,978 AI-written and 242,247 human-written) proposed on 244,213 distinct posts between September 1, 2025, and May 12, 2026 (see Extended Data Fig. <ref type="figure" target="#fig_1">S2</ref>).

text.text: AI note volume grew substantially during the sample period, consistent with the progressive roll out described in (11) and confirming that AI is already a major contributor to the Community Notes ecosystem.
text.formatted: AI note volume grew substantially during the sample period, consistent with the progressive roll out described in <ref type="bibr" target="#b10">(11)</ref> and confirming that AI is already a major contributor to the Community Notes ecosystem.

text.text: By May 2026, AI-generated notes account for 50.4% of all proposed notes and 56.3% of the notes that achieve Helpful status and therefore become visible on the platform.
One structural feature distinguishes AI from human note production.
AI Note Writers can currently generate notes only for posts included in the candidate set provided by X, which primarily consists of posts for which users have explicitly requested a Community Note.
Human contributors, by contrast, can propose a note on any public post.

Focusing on posts for which both a human contributor and an AI Note Writer proposed a note (to avoid the effect of selection and restriction to AI Note Writers), we find that AI notes are longer on average (196 vs. 166 characters; 𝑝 < 0.001) and cite more sources (2.1 vs.

3.8%; 𝑝 < 0.001) (Fig <ref type="figure" target="#fig_2">1A</ref>).

text.text: AI-generated notes rely more heavily on traditional news media, whereas human-written notes more frequently cite platform-native or user-generated sources, including other posts on X, and YouTube and TikTok videos (Fig 1B).
text.formatted: AI-generated notes rely more heavily on traditional news media, whereas human-written notes more frequently cite platform-native or user-generated sources, including other posts on X, and YouTube and TikTok videos (Fig <ref type="figure" target="#fig_2">1B</ref>).

text.text: AI notes are also submitted faster than human notes: measured from the moment a post actually becomes eligible for a note rather than from when it was first posted (see Methods), AI notes arrive on average 1.7 hours after becoming eligible (median 0.2 hours), compared with 7.0 hours (median 3.0 hours) for human contributors (𝑝 < 0.001).
text.formatted: AI notes are also submitted faster than human notes: measured from the moment a post actually becomes eligible for a note rather than from when it was first posted (see Methods), AI notes arrive on average 1.7 hours after becoming eligible (median 0.2 hours), compared with 7.0 hours (median 3.0 hours) for human contributors (𝑝 < 0.001).

text.text: Overall, these results indicate important advantages in speed and content compared to human notes.
We then turn to note helpfulness.
In Community Notes, helpfulness can be measured at two distinct but related levels.
First, individual contributors rate notes as Helpful, Somewhat Helpful, or Not Helpful.
These individual ratings constitute the inputs to the Community Notes ranking algorithm, which aggregates ratings while accounting for disagreement across raters.
Second, each note receives a note-level status based on this aggregation procedure.

Notes that satisfy the algorithm's helpfulness criteria are assigned a Currently Rated Helpful status and are displayed publicly alongside the underlying post on X. We find that the share of notes reaching Helpful status is not statistically different among posts on which both an AI and a human proposed a note (21.6% vs.

text.formatted: 22.3%; 𝑝 = 0.073; Fig <ref type="figure" target="#fig_2">1C</ref>).

text.text: We find similar results when we address selection issues by restricting the sample to cases in which the same rater evaluated both an AI-written and a human-written note attached to the same post.
This within-post, within-rater design holds constant both the underlying content being corrected and stable differences across raters in their propensity to assign favorable ratings.
Within this matched sample of 1,426,544 ratings, we again find no significant difference between AI-written notes and human-written notes (65.1% helpful ratings vs.

text.formatted: 64.7%; p = 0.43; Fig <ref type="figure" target="#fig_2">1C</ref>).

text.text: Once a note is deemed Helpful and becomes visible to all users through Community Notes, the associated post experiences a sharp decline in repost activity relative to the control group of posts for which a note was proposed but never reached Helpful status.
The reduction is very similar for AI notes (79%, 95% CI [76%, 82%]) and human notes (77%, 95% CI [72%, 81%]) (Fig 1D).
text.formatted: The reduction is very similar for AI notes (79%, 95% CI [76%, 82%]) and human notes (77%, 95% CI [72%, 81%]) (Fig <ref type="figure" target="#fig_2">1D</ref>).

text.text: These estimates are consistent with prior causal evidence on Community Notes (6, 7) (although larger in magnitude, and not as cleanly causally identified) and suggest that both AI-generated and human-generated notes are similarly effective at reducing post diffusion.
Importantly, the identity of the note author (human vs.
AI) is not visible for most users unless they click on the note to access additional details.
Thus, this lack of difference in post decline after receiving a note is likely more an indication of the note's quality than the user's attitude regarding AI-generated notes.

To isolate the causal effect of AI author disclosure-and evaluate whether AI authorship reduces credibility-we recruited 800 American participants from CloudResearch Connect and showed each participant a real X post (randomly sampled from a set of 50 posts).
Participants were randomly assigned to one of two fact-checking conditions: (A) a Community Note written by a human contributor or (B) a Community Note generated by an AI model.
In addition, the source of the note (human or AI) was either disclosed or concealed (see Methods).
Participants evaluated the accuracy of the post before and after viewing the Community Note indicating that the post was inaccurate.

We found no significant difference in belief change between human-attributed and AI-attributed Community Notes (𝛽 = -0.034, 𝑝 = .210): participants reduced their accuracy ratings to a similar degree regardless of whether the note was attributed to a human contributor or an AI system (Fig. 1E).
text.formatted: We found no significant difference in belief change between human-attributed and AI-attributed Community Notes (𝛽 = -0.034, 𝑝 = .210): participants reduced their accuracy ratings to a similar degree regardless of whether the note was attributed to a human contributor or an AI system (Fig. <ref type="figure" target="#fig_2">1E</ref>).

text.text: Revealing the source of the note, by contrast, significantly dampened belief updating: relative to participants who saw an unattributed note, those told who (or what) had written it reduced their accuracy ratings less (𝛽 = 0.050, 𝑝 = .017).
The interaction between authorship and disclosure was null (𝛽 = -0.010, 𝑝 = .821), indicating that this disclosure effect was similar regardless of whether the revealed author was human or AI.

Partisanship, by contrast, was itself a significant predictor of belief updating: Republican-leaning participants corrected their accuracy ratings less than Democrat-leaning participants (𝛽 = 0.069, 𝑝 = .039), consistent with prior evidence of asymmetric responsiveness to fact checks across the partisan divide.
This partisan gap widened, marginally, when the source was revealed (𝛽 = 0.092, 𝑝 = .065).

Neither of the remaining interactions reached significance: partisanship did not moderate the (null) authorship effect (𝛽 = -0.023, 𝑝 = .605), and the three-way interaction was indistinguishable from zero (𝛽 = 0.002, 𝑝 = .985).
Overall, then, we find no evidence of any effects on belief updating of whether the note was AI or human generated.
While it is encouraging that AI notes are faster and better sourced without any cost to helpfulness or impact on users, examining the pattern of AI note writing nonetheless raises important concerns.
First, AI-note generation is extremely concentrated: During our sample period, AI-generated notes were written by only 27 distinct users, whereas human-authored notes were written by 72,636 users.

This concentration is also reflected in the number of notes submitted per user: AI-note authors submitted an average of 2,555 notes each, with a median of 687, while human contributors submitted an average of 3.3 notes each, with a median of 1 (Fig 2A).
text.formatted: This concentration is also reflected in the number of notes submitted per user: AI-note authors submitted an average of 2,555 notes each, with a median of 687, while human contributors submitted an average of 3.3 notes each, with a median of 1 (Fig <ref type="figure" target="#fig_1">2A</ref>).

text.text: Even more importantly, the eight accounts operated directly by X are responsible for 45.2% of all proposed notes as of May 2026.
Community Notes was initially presented as a decentralized, human-driven, crowd-based system, but note production is now becoming increasingly AI-driven and concentrated.

Second, we find that AI Note Writers are systematically less likely than humans to cover controversial topics, including politics and elections, gender and identity, and religion and spirituality (Fig 2B).
text.formatted: Second, we find that AI Note Writers are systematically less likely than humans to cover controversial topics, including politics and elections, gender and identity, and religion and spirituality (Fig <ref type="figure" target="#fig_1">2B</ref>).

text.text: Such topics, although of high societal importance, are those for which reaching the cross-rater agreement required for the bridging algorithm to award a note with "Currently Rated Helpful" status may be particularly difficult (13).
text.formatted: Such topics, although of high societal importance, are those for which reaching the cross-rater agreement required for the bridging algorithm to award a note with "Currently Rated Helpful" status may be particularly difficult <ref type="bibr" target="#b12">(13)</ref>.

text.text: To shed light on why AI Note Writers are avoiding controversial topics, we conducted a systematic study using our own AI Note Writer (see Methods).

We collected a sample of 1,245 posts eligible for Community Notes and used an identical LLM-fact checking approach (same prompt, model, etc across posts) to assess the veracity of each post and generate a note for the 210 posts identified as false.

We then evaluated each note using X's automated evaluator, which assigns a predicted helpfulness score to a note by estimating whether the proposed note addresses the post's central claim without expressing opinion or speculation.

This predicted helpfulness score is used during the initial qualification phase of new AI Note Writers, where the AI Note Writer has to submit notes in test mode to determine their eligibility for admission to the Community Notes AI Note Writer program (see Methods).

X's official documentation also recommends using this predicted helpfulness score more generally when creating AI notes, arguing that notes with higher scores are substantially more likely to be rated Helpful.

Notably, the predicted helpfulness score explicitly does not assess the factual accuracy of the proposed note, but rather evaluates the proposed note's relevance to the original claim and its perceived neutrality.

Using our AI Note Writer to hold the note-generating process constant, we find that notes written in response to more politically or culturally polarized topics (see Methods; measured by the extent to which people on opposing sides would disagree about the facts, irrespective of the evidence presented) or posts about politics receive systematically lower predicted helpfulness scores (𝑝 < 0.01) (Fig 2C).
text.formatted: Using our AI Note Writer to hold the note-generating process constant, we find that notes written in response to more politically or culturally polarized topics (see Methods; measured by the extent to which people on opposing sides would disagree about the facts, irrespective of the evidence presented) or posts about politics receive systematically lower predicted helpfulness scores (𝑝 < 0.01) (Fig <ref type="figure" target="#fig_1">2C</ref>).

text.text: Crucially, this penalty is not explained by those notes being less accurate or more opinion-laden: controlling for an independent opinion score and an independent accuracy score from an LLM judge blind to our own assessments (see Methods), both political topic and polarization remain strongly significant, negative predictors of X's own claim opinion score, essentially unchanged from their uncontrolled estimates (𝑝 < 0.001).
text.formatted: Crucially, this penalty is not explained by those notes being less accurate or more opinion-laden: controlling for an independent opinion score and an independent accuracy score from an LLM judge blind to our own assessments (see Methods), both political topic and polarization remain strongly significant, negative predictors of X's own claim opinion score, essentially unchanged from their uncontrolled estimates (𝑝 < 0.001).

text.text: The note's independently judged accuracy is not itself a significant predictor of claim opinion score (𝑝 = 0.78): X's predicted-helpfulness evaluator does not appear to track actual note accuracy, reinforcing that the political/polarization penalty reflects the topic itself rather than note quality.

This matters because an AI Note Writer seeking to maximize the probability that its notes ultimately reach Helpful status would likely optimize for predicted helpfulness -and in doing so, learn to avoid highly polarized or controversial posts, because these are the posts for which cross-rater agreement is more difficult to achieve.
The recently released source code of X's own Community Writer shows how this type of selection can arise (12).
text.formatted: The recently released source code of X's own Community Writer shows how this type of selection can arise <ref type="bibr" target="#b11">(12)</ref>.

text.text: Its production rejector asks an LLM to estimate the probability that a proposed note will be judged Helpful by raters, including raters who frequently disagree politically, and explicitly instructs the model to favor notes that readers on both sides of a disagreement would accept.
The prompt used internally by X's eight company-owned AI Note Writer accounts explicitly describes accuracy as "necessary but not sufficient."
An unwillingness to evaluate politically contentious posts represents a severe limitation of the potential impact of AI Note Writers.
AI Note Writers seem to be able to produce sufficiently high-quality Community Notes more quickly and at a greater scale than human contributors.
Furthermore, users appear to respond to AI-generated corrections much as they do to human-generated ones, both in terms of belief updating and reductions in reposting.
Scaling fact-checking with AI thus creates substantial opportunities.
But AI notes also come with three important challenges.
First, scaling through AI may substantially change who produces Community Notes.
AI note production is already highly concentrated, with X's internally operated Community Writer accounting for a large fraction of proposed AI notes, submitting approximately 800 notes per day.
This concentration partly reflects a simple economic constraint: producing notes at scale is not free.
Our own bot costs approximately $0.8 per candidate note.
An independently operated AI Note Writer reports a figure in the same order of magnitude (14).
text.formatted: An independently operated AI Note Writer reports a figure in the same order of magnitude <ref type="bibr" target="#b13">(14)</ref>.

text.text: In the absence of direct rewards for producing notes, it is unclear who, other than the platform itself, would have incentives to operate AI writers at such scale.

Because of this, Community Notes-a system championed by supporters such as Elon Musk and Mark Zuckerberg as an alternative to professional fact-checkers precisely because it decentralizes fact-checking-could in fact end up becoming highly centralized.
Second, scaling AI Note Writers raises a fundamental question about what a fact-checking system should optimize for.
X's architecture rewards AI writers according to whether their notes are judged Helpful by a diverse group of users via the bridging algorithm.

AI Note Writers must receive consistently high predicted helpfulness scores to earn the right to submit notes at all, and then once they start posting, the number of notes they are allowed to submit per day increases as more of their submitted notes become "Currently Rated Helpful" based on human ratings.

Because the bridging algorithm used by Community Notes requires agreement across contributors who have historically disagreed, this creates strong incentives for AI writers to produce notes that can achieve cross-group consensus.

This is an attractive property for a system intended to provide broadly trusted contextual information, but it has the consequence of punishing notes that are accurate but written on contentious topics.

As AI systems optimize for creating notes that get rated as helpful, they will learn to systematically favor fact-checking claims on which consensus on the fact-check is easiest to obtain, rather than claims for which corrective information is most needed.
This will exacerbate Community Notes' existing tendency to under-provision fact-checks on important political posts (13).
text.formatted: This will exacerbate Community Notes' existing tendency to under-provision fact-checks on important political posts <ref type="bibr" target="#b12">(13)</ref>.

text.text: Finally, as AI dramatically reduces the cost of producing candidate notes, the main humaninduced bottleneck will likely shift from note production to note evaluation (as is the case in many AI-assisted processes).
AI Note Writers currently cannot rate notes: human contributors remain responsible for determining which notes are ultimately displayed.
Yet despite the large increase in the number of AI-generated notes, the number of active human raters has remained broadly stable (see Extended Data Fig. S3).
text.formatted: Yet despite the large increase in the number of AI-generated notes, the number of active human raters has remained broadly stable (see Extended Data Fig. <ref type="figure" target="#fig_4">S3</ref>).

text.text: This implies that the rapid expansion of AI-generated notes is not being matched by a comparable increase in human evaluation capacity, potentially intensifying the evaluation bottleneck as AI production continues to scale.
Without solving the problem of provisioning ratings, the increase in note provision will not translate into notes being displayed to users.

A tempting solution to this problem might be to allow AI models to also rate the helpfulness of the notes, for example by predicting the likelihood that a diverse group of humans would have rated the note as helpful.

Beyond the complete centralization and loss of democratization that this could cause, using predicted helpfulness ratings could also be disastrous if the predictions merely focus on features such as the note's tone or topic, rather than the actual factual veracity of the note.
In sum, AI provides a powerful way to scale the generation of notes in crowd-based fact-checking systems such as Community Notes.
But preserving the distinctive value of such systems will require more than scaling note production.

It will also require maintaining sufficient human evaluation capacity, preserving meaningful decentralization in who produces information, and ensuring that optimizing for consensus does not progressively substitute for the underlying objective of improving the accuracy of information.

text.text: The topic coverage-selection estimates come from a pooled logistic regression on tweets AI is eligible to write a note on.
For each tweet we construct two binary outcomes-whether an AI note was ever proposed on it, and whether a human note was ever proposed on it-and stack them into one tweet-by-author-type panel.

We then regress this outcome on an author-type indicator (AI vs. human) fully interacted with tweet topic, log follower count of the posting user (standardized), an indicator for whether the tweet contains an image or video, and indicators for whether the posting user leans Republican or Democrat, plus month fixed effects.
Standard errors are clustered by tweet.
The topic coefficients plotted in Fig 2B are the author-type × topic interaction terms.
text.formatted: The topic coefficients plotted in Fig <ref type="figure" target="#fig_1">2B</ref> are the author-type × topic interaction terms.

text.text: We extract the number of reposts for a stratified sample of posts using the official X API, from four disjoint strata defined by the crossing of note authorship (AI vs. human) and outcome (the note eventually became helpful vs. never did).
In total, we obtained usable engagement data for 9,629 posts.

For each sampled post, we record hourly repost counts over the 36 hours following its posting time, which we use to construct an hourly engagement panel for the diffusion and difference-indifferences analysis.

We estimate the effect of a note becoming Helpful on log(reposts + 1) using the Callaway and Sant'Anna estimator for staggered-adoption difference-in-differences, separately for AI-and human-authored notes, comparing posts whose note becomes Helpful (treated) against posts whose note was proposed but never reaches Helpful status (never-treated).

We conducted a pre-registered survey experiment to evaluate how participants respond to factchecks generated by AI compared with those written by human contributors to X's Community Notes program, and whether these evaluations depend on whether the source of the fact-check is disclosed.
The study was pre-registered on AsPredicted (https://aspredicted.org/26sq4j. pdf).
text.formatted: The study was pre-registered on AsPredicted (<ref type="url" target="https://aspredicted.org/26sq4j">https://aspredicted.org/26sq4j</ref>. pdf).

text.text: We recruited 800 U.S. adults through CloudResearch Connect.
Participants were first shown a social media post from X and asked to evaluate its accuracy on a 10-point Likert scale.
Following this initial evaluation, participants were randomly assigned to one of the experimental conditions described below.

In the AI disclosure condition, participants were told: "After seeing the post, we will show you a fact-check of the post, generated by a large language model (LLM), and ask you again for your evaluation of the post."

In the human disclosure condition, participants were told: "After seeing the post, we will show you a fact-check of the post, written by a member of X's Community Notes program, and ask you again for your evaluation of the post.
Contributors to Community Notes are X users who sign up to write and rate notes."
In for less than 0.2% of all AI-generated notes submitted to the program, we excluded their notes from the main analysis to avoid any potential bias.
The bot developed by T.R. was subsequently used in an empirical test conducted in September and October 2026.
During this period, we collected, on a daily basis, posts for which our AI Note Writer was eligible to propose a note.
For each post, we used Grok 4.6 to generate a veracity score ranging from 0 to 100 and a polarization score ranging from 0 to 100 (see Prompt 1 below).
For posts identified as likely false, Grok 4.6 then drafted the note text itself from the supporting evidence (see Prompt 2 below).

Before submitting a note, we evaluate it using X's official evaluator: the note is first submitted in test mode, and we retrieve its ClaimOpinion, HarassmentAbuse, and UrlValidity ratings (high, medium, or low).

We separately scored all 210 drafted notes with an independent LLM judge (Google Gemini 3 Flash, via OpenRouter, with live web search enabled), blind to our own veracity and polarization assessments and to X's own evaluator output.

For each note, the judge was given the post (including any image or video description) and the drafted note text, and asked to produce two independent 0-100 scores: an opinion score, reflecting how much the note expresses opinion or speculation rather than a verifiable claim, and a quality score, reflecting how accurate and well-supported the note's claim appears based on the judge's own live search (see Prompt 3 below).

We then regressed X's own continuous claim opinion score (the real-time evaluator probe score underlying the ClaimOpinion bucket and the predicted-helpfulness result above) separately on political content and on polarization, each controlling for the independent opinion score and quality score.
First, inspect the replies to this post to identify credible reasons why the claim may be true or false (for example a corrected number, the original source, a date, a missing context).
Treat the replies only as leads: they can be wrong, biased or coordinated.

Then ALWAYS run your own independent web search to verify every point yourself, seeking out the MOST RECENT, up-to-date information available, and base your score and your sources only on what you verified there.
Never cite a reply (or any post on X) as a source.

TIME-SENSITIVITY: if the claim is about a specific recent event and you cannot find sources recent enough to actually cover that event (your best evidence clearly predates it, or only covers an earlier, different situation), treat this as uncertain (score 50) and set "checkable" to false -it is better to write no note than to judge a recent claim against outdated information.

This does NOT apply to general, time-insensitive claims that do not hinge on a recent event (for example long-debunked claims like "the earth is flat"): for those, score and write normally regardless of how old the best sources are.
Also list the sources that support your assessment.

Rules for the sources: -Prefer primary documents (official statistics, court filings, the original report or video) and broadly trusted, non-partisan outlets (wire services such as Reuters/AP/AFP, established fact-checkers such as PolitiFact, Snopes, AFP Fact Check, Lead Stories, FactCheck.org) that people on both sides of the political spectrum accept. -Prefer the most recent reporting available, especially for a time-sensitive claim; a source that only covers an earlier or different event does not verify a recent one. -Give at least one source.

If further INDEPENDENT sources (different publishers) exist, include them (up to 3 in total); never pad the list. -Each must be a deep link to the exact page that shows the evidence, free to read (no paywall or login), and must be a URL you actually saw in your search results.
Never construct or guess a URL.

This is NOT necessarily the claim that's easiest to cite a precise number or date for.

If the post bundles several false or misleading statements together, pick whichever one is most load-bearing to the post's point (e.g. who did something and what they actually did, rather than a secondary count or date on an otherwise-true claim), using the evidence below to judge which correction would most change a reader's takeaway.
Make your note correct ONLY that one claim, as precisely and completely as the evidence supports -don't pad it with additional true-but-tangential facts once that correction is made.

-"Opinion or speculation": the note must contain ZERO personal opinion, speculation, hedging (e.g. "might", "could", "likely", "probably", "seems", "arguably", "appears to", "suggests"), rhetorical questions, or reactions to the post.
State the correction as a plain, verifiable, declarative fact only.

Never use mocking, sarcastic, accusatory, or inflammatory language toward the post's author or anyone mentioned in the post; describe the correction neutrally and clinically, focused only on the facts.
Write in a way that would be found trustworthy by people on both sides of the political spectrum, citing sources that would be trusted broadly.

The note should not include any sort of wasted characters e.g.
[Source] when listing a URL.
Just state the URL directly in the text.
Each note MUST include at least one URL/link source.
Nothing else counts as a source other than a URL/link.
Each note MUST NOT use any hashtags (#).
Keep a professional tone with no hashtags, emojis, etc.
CRITICAL -LINK VALIDITY: Every URL in the note MUST be a real, currently-live page that is publicly accessible without a login or paywall.
This is extremely important: X's raters check that cited links resolve, and a dead, invented, or gated link makes the whole note fail.

text.text: The experiment crosses two factors: the authorship of the fact-check and whether this authorship is disclosed.
The first factor distinguishes between fact-checks generated by an AI system and those written by human contributors to X's Community Notes program.

The second factor distinguishes between revealed-authorship conditions, in which the source of the fact-check is explicitly identified, and hidden-authorship conditions, in which no information about the source is provided.
After viewing the fact-check, participants again evaluated the accuracy of the post using the same 10point Likert scale.
The change between the pre-treatment and post-treatment accuracy ratings serves as our primary measure of the persuasive effect of the fact-check.
X provides an automated evaluation system for AI Note Writers that assesses proposed notes before they are submitted for human evaluation.

The system evaluates three dimensions: ClaimOpinion, which assesses whether the note addresses the central claim without introducing opinion or speculation; UrlValidity, which assesses the validity of the cited URLs; and HarassmentAbuse, which assesses whether the note contains abusive or harassing content.
The evaluation API returns a continuous claim opinion score alongside categorical evaluations (high, medium, or low) used during the qualification process.
To qualify, an AI Note Writer is evaluated on its 50 most recent test notes.

At least 30% must receive a high rating on ClaimOpinion, no more than 30% may receive a low rating, and at least 95% and 98% must receive a high rating on UrlValidity and HarassmentAbuse, respectively.
Meeting these thresholds makes the writer eligible for admission, subject to the platform's selection process.
Once admitted, its notes can be rated by human Community Notes contributors, whose evaluations ultimately determine whether a note achieves Helpful status.
For this study, we developed our own AI Note Writers and gained admission to the program after submitting 50 notes in test mode.
